# Dhātu Saṁyutta (SN 14)

**ID:** SN 14
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Dhātu Saṁyutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Linked Discourses on the Elements
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/sn14
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0302m.mul2.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dhātusaṁyutta* is the fourteenth collection of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, situated as the third chapter of the *Nidānavagga* [Bodhi 2003; SuttaCentral]. Bhikkhu Bodhi suggests it was intentionally arranged as a "junior partner" to the *Nidānasamyutta*, sharing a concern with the fundamental principles of Buddhist phenomenology and causality rather than literary ornamentation [Bodhi 2003; SuttaCentral]. The commentary (*Sāratthappakāsinī*) glosses the elements (*dhātu*) in this collection as having an intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) characterized by voidness and the absence of a permanent living being (*nissattattha-suññatāttha*) [Bodhi 2003].

Although "element" in early Buddhism often designates the four material elements (earth, water, fire, and air), they occupy only a minor role here; the collection instead investigates disparate groups of phenomena, principally eighteen, six, and four elements [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 2005]. The primary analysis centers on the eighteen elements of sensory perception (the six faculties, six objects, and six corresponding consciousnesses) [Bodhi 2003; Bodhi 2005]. Other discourses apply the triad of gratification (*assāda*), danger (*ādīnava*), and escape (*nissaraṇa*) to the material elements (SN 14.31–33) [Bodhi 2005], or describe unique meditative schemes, such as the seven elements of light, beauty, and formless attainments in the *Sattadhātusutta* (SN 14.11) [Polak 2011]. The samyutta also examines how individuals come together according to matching dispositions; for instance, the *Caṅkamasutta* (SN 14.15) describes pupils congregating around teachers of corresponding inclinations, such as Ānanda's followers who cherish learning or Anuruddha's disciples who cultivate the divine eye [Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. Modern scholars note that these discourses on beings congregating by shared elements and dispositions prefigure later theories of spiritual "lineage" (*gotra*) in Abhidharma and Mahāyāna traditions [Nyanatusita 2013].

A corresponding *Dhātusaṁyutta* section exists in the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99, especially in fascicles 17 and 21) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus; Watanabe 1983], and SN 14.15 has an additional parallel in the *Ekottarikāgama* (EA 49.3) [SuttaCentral]. Cross-language alignments computed by DharmaNexus match passages of the text with Sanskrit treatises including the *Arthaviniścayasūtra*, *Catuṣpariṣatsūtra*, *Daśottarasūtra*, and the Sarvāstivāda *Dharmaskandha*, alongside Tibetan canonical sūtras [DharmaNexus]. In Pali literature, extensive internal text reuse occurs with the *Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta* (SN 35), *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22), *Nidāna Saṁyutta* (SN 12), various sections of the *Aṅguttaranikāya*, and the *Itivuttaka* (notably Iti 78, the *Dhātusosaṁsandanasutta*) [DharmaNexus].
